t: LeetCode 3164 – Find the Number of Good Pairs II
o: We must count pairs (i, j) where nums1[i] is divisible by nums2[j] * k. In example 2, k = 3 turns nums2 into targets {6, 12}; only 12 divides 12, giving 2 pairs. Brute force over all pairs is O(n·m) = 10^10, far too slow for n, m up to 10^5. However values are capped at 10^6, which invites counting by value: if we know how many nums1 elements equal each value, one nums2 target v contributes cnt1[multiple] for every multiple of v.
k: Multiply every nums2 value by k first; then we only need divisibility by plain integers.
Counting by value lets us trade pair enumeration for harmonic-series enumeration over 10^6.

a.i: Build frequency maps of nums1 and of k·nums2. For each distinct target v, every nums1 element that is a multiple of v forms a good pair, so sweep multiples v, 2v, 3v, … up to 10^6 and add cnt2[v] · cnt1[multiple]. The total work is Σ 10^6/v over distinct v, which is comfortably fast.
s: Build Counter of nums1 and Counter of nums2 scaled by k.
For each v in the scaled counter, iterate multiples m = v, 2v, … ≤ 10^6 and add cnt2[v] * cnt1[m].
a.t: O(M log M) where M = 10^6 — the harmonic sweep over multiples dominates
a.sp: O(n + m) for the frequency maps

a.n: Approach 2: Divisor enumeration per distinct nums1 value
a.i: Symmetric idea: for each distinct x in nums1, x is divisible by target v exactly when v is a divisor of x. Enumerate divisors of x in O(√x) and look them up in the scaled nums2 counter. This is preferable when nums1 has few distinct values.
s: Build Counter of k·nums2 and Counter of nums1.
For each distinct x, enumerate divisor pairs (d, x/d) up to √x and add their counts times cnt1[x].
a.t: O(D · √V) where D = distinct values in nums1 and V ≤ 10^6

w: Prefer Approach 1 in an interview: it is simpler and its harmonic bound is easy to argue. Pitfalls: remember to multiply nums2 by k before counting, watch overflow (pairs can reach ~10^10, hence long long / safe ints), and deduplicate work by iterating distinct values. Follow-ups: what if values reached 10^9 (divisor approach with factorization) or if k could be 0?
